title: Automatic classification of medical image modality and anatomical location using convolutional neural network
abstract: Modern radiologic images comply with DICOM (digital imaging and communications in medicine) standard, which, upon conversion to other image format, would lose its image detail and information such as patient demographics or type of image modality that DICOM format carries. As there is a growing interest in using large amount of image data for research purpose and acquisition of large amount of medical image is now a standard practice in the clinical setting, efficient handling and storage of large amount of image data is important in both the clinical and research setting. In this study, four classes of images were created, namely, CT (computed tomography) of abdomen, CT of brain, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and MRI of spine. After converting these images into JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group) format, our proposed CNN architecture could automatically classify these 4 groups of medical images by both their image modality and anatomic location. We achieved excellent overall classification accuracy in both validation and test sets (> 99.5%), specificity and F1 score (> 99%) in each category of this dataset which contained both diseased and normal images. Our study has shown that using CNN for medical image classification is a promising methodology and could work on non-DICOM images, which could potentially save image processing time and storage space.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2021 PLoS ONE article has shown clear scholarly uptake in medical-imaging and AI research, with 36 citations in OpenAlex, placement in the top 10% of its field and year, and 37 documented downstream reuse events. Its influence is concentrated in technical and clinical imaging venues, suggesting the paper has been used as a practical reference point for automated image classification workflows.

Full narrative

The strongest signal for this article is sustained academic reuse. OpenAlex records 36 citations, and the field-normalized percentile places it in the top 10% for its year. The citing literature is not limited to a single niche: it spans journal articles, conference papers, and a small number of preprints, which points to a method that has been taken up across both established and fast-moving research settings.

The citation landscape is especially telling in medical imaging and AI-adjacent venues such as Scientific Reports, the Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine, Biomedical Signal Processing and Control, Sensors, and Lecture Notes in Computer Science. Recent citing works show that the paper continues to be used in current discussions of modality classification, CT/MRI metadata prediction, privacy-preserving imaging, and multimodal radiology evaluation, indicating that the contribution remains relevant as imaging AI evolves.

Beyond citations, the record shows 37 instances of downstream reuse, including 30 journal articles, four conference papers, two preprints, and one biomedical article mention in Europe PMC. This pattern suggests the article functions as reusable methodological infrastructure rather than only a one-off result. The surrounding concepts in the citing literature also cluster around radiomics, medical imaging analysis, and AI for cancer and COVID-19-related imaging tasks, which aligns with the paper’s focus on automating image modality and anatomical-location classification from radiologic data.

The paper’s reach is largely scholarly and technical. OpenAIRE lists the article as gold open access with multiple open instances, which likely supports discoverability and reuse. At the same time, the broader public attention record is modest in the sources available here, so the main story is one of research uptake rather than wide public discourse.

There is also post-publication scrutiny in the record, with two PubPeer threads. That does not by itself resolve the paper’s reliability or influence, but it is part of the visible reception history and should be read alongside the citation and reuse signals. Overall, the article appears to have established a durable footprint in medical-imaging AI, particularly as a reference for automated classification of image modality and anatomy.
